paragraphs.text: Yesterday our sermon gave itself both to the wrestling match against the heretics and to the contest for the glory of the Only-begotten. It did not aim to reveal hidden things, but to acknowledge his grace with gratitude. Christ is not made great by what we say. Rather, because we have been made great, we gratefully proclaim the kindness we have received. It would be utterly absurd for us, who have been treated so well in deed, to repay that kindness with silence, especially when the prophet David urges us on, saying, as you have just heard: "Let all the earth worship you and sing praise to you." We sing hymns to God not to confer honour on him but to gain honour for ourselves. We glorify God not to bestow glory on him but to clothe ourselves with immortal glory. "For those who glorify me," he says, "I will glorify, and those who despise me shall be despised." Through the contest it fought as best it could, our sermon taught that no one may overstep the bounds of God's glory: not human beings on earth, not angels in heaven, not archangels, not principalities, not the cherubim, not the seraphim. And you remember (I know well that the keen learners among my hearers remember) how our discussion of these things was carried through. But today, brothers, the King of glory himself has foretold his own cross, and the apostle, following the Saviour's royal voice, has expounded the doctrine of the cross. For the Lord said to his disciples: "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of enemies." And Paul, rebuking the Galatians, wrote: "Who has bewitched you, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed among you as crucified?" Since, then, the Lord's royal voice has spoken, and the teaching of his faithful servant has followed in the royal footsteps, I think it necessary that we too, as far as we are able, should say what is fitting about the Lord's saving cross. We do not hope to match its worth, but to pay our debt as far as we can. What, then, does the Saviour say? "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man is handed over." The conqueror of death foretells his suffering. He who destroys death by the cross announces the cross beforehand. He announces the struggle in advance so that he may proclaim the victory. Here again, set yourself to consider the Master's words. See with what authority he says: "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man is handed over to be crucified." Yet the one who foretells these things, once he is in the contest itself, sets aside the dignity of his authority and disowns the rank of his Godhead, saying: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." Do you not see the discord? Consider the dispensation. But let us return to our subject. He says to the disciples: "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man is handed over." See how guarded his words are. Where he proclaims suffering, he points to the human nature: "The Son of Man is handed over." For the visible body suffers, while the rank of the Godhead, perceived by the mind, gives life. The form of the body, brothers, is dissolved by death, but the power of the one who dwells within raises up what is dissolved. He himself was the one dissolved according to the body, and he himself raised up what was dissolved according to the spirit. For he says: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." "See, we are going up to Jerusalem." Those who follow Christ can never go down anywhere, but always go up. Besides, the road from Jericho to Jerusalem was literally an ascent, and in a spiritual sense the passion led to the ascent of the resurrection. For he was calling Adam, who had fallen into Hades, up to heaven, and he raised the image that lay on the ground to the heights. "We are going up to Jerusalem." Where God is, there is the ascent of virtue; where wickedness is, there is the descent of lawlessness. That is why David says of those who live virtuously: "Blessed are all who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ever and ever. Blessed is the man whose help comes from you; your ascents are in his heart." "Your ascents" means the devout and uplifted thoughts that lead to the heights those who think rightly about God. There is, then, a road of self-control that leads up on high and a road of justice that carries one on high. Indeed every road of piety, so to speak, leads the lover of God by the hand to that height of which those from the nations said: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob." Where the word of piety is found there is ascent, but where wickedness is found there is, as all agree, descent. The prophet David bears witness to this when he says: "Rescue me from those who go down into the pit," and again: "You who lift me up from the gates of death." So even the words "we are going up" are not superfluous. "See, we are going up." And yet he goes to the passion alone. Why, then, does he say "we are going up," as if in common? Because the suffering is mine, but the salvation is shared by all people. That is why the divine apostle uttered that noble saying, full of wonder, which you have just heard: "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." Moreover, wishing to show the fruit of the cross as well, he added straight away in what follows: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."

Here pay close attention, so that the quarry of truth does not escape you. The Jews will object at once (Paul speaks of them: "the enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction"), and sometimes they will say to simple people: "If the one who hangs on a tree is cursed, how do you expect a blessing to be given to you by the cursed one? How do you look for life from one who fell under death? What is plain to see, as your teacher Paul himself admitted, is a curse; for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. If, then, it is written and attested, how is a blessing given by the cursed one to those who cherish the cross?" This is what the Jew, the enemy of the cross of Christ, always puts forward and says. So if he says to you, "How does the cursed one give a blessing?", say to him: "How was it that in the wilderness the serpents were biting your forefathers, and Moses made a bronze image of a serpent, set it up on a stake, and said: Let everyone who has been bitten by the serpent look to the serpent, and he will be saved?" "And what," he says, "has this to do with the subject?" On the contrary, it is very closely related. Or have you not heard God say: "Cursed are you above all the beasts of the earth"? How, then, did the image of the cursed one bring life to your forefathers? I repeat the words in order to establish the sense. If you think it impossible for a blessing to spring from the cursed one (since "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree"), how did the image of the cursed serpent, which was told "Cursed are you above all the beasts," bring salvation to the people lying in calamity? Would it not have been more credible to say: "If any of you is bitten, let him look up to heaven, to God, and he will be saved"? And even leaving aside looking to heaven, could he not have said: "If anyone is bitten, let him look at the lampstand of light, and he will be saved," or "let him look at the table set with the holy loaves, and he will be saved," or at the altar, or the veil, or the ark, or the image of the cherubim, or the mercy seat? But the great lawgiver brought in none of these. He set up only the image of the cross, and did so by means of the cursed serpent. Why, then, O Jew, does Moses do this? Why does he cast a serpent in metal, when he says in the law: "You shall not make a carved image or a cast one"? But why do I say this to a man without understanding? I put the question to the lawgiver himself: "Tell me, most faithful servant of God, do you do what you forbid? Do you build what you tear down? You who say, 'You shall not make a carved image or a cast one,' do you cast and carve a serpent?" "I laid down those laws," he says, "to cut away the materials of impiety and to lead this people away from all idolatry. But now I cast the serpent to prefigure the image of the dispensation of the cross. I level the road in advance for the apostles; I rehearse beforehand that great and strange symbol, the cross." To see that this argument is not forced, listen to the Lord confirming that ancient image and taking it upon himself. Speaking with Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, as a teacher of the people and one able to grasp the deeper meaning of the dispensation, he says: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." Tell me, then, you senseless Jew, was that not bronze? Dead matter had power to conquer death because it bore the figure of the cross, and is the very reality of the cross not believed? And this after the conversion of the world, after the reign of piety that has shone out over the whole world, after the faith of the nations, after the raising of churches, after so much struggle, so much ascetic discipline, so much progress in the angelic way of life? But it has been clearly shown how the enemies of the cross are barred from taunting us with the figure of the cursed one. So much for them. But let us, the faithful, examine among ourselves and test the precise meaning of the words. Why did the Lord make the image of that dispensation by means of a serpent and not by something else? Against our opponents in debate, the example of the cursed serpent is enough. But to persuade the children of piety, we must explain why the figure of the cursed serpent became an image of the Christ whom we worship. So we must speak with diligence, and you must listen with eagerness.

The figure of the serpent, brothers, was an image of the dispensation of the cross. That figure had the image and appearance of a serpent, but not a serpent's venom and malice. In the same way the Saviour, as the divine apostle says, appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, yet remained free of all sin. So too blessed Isaiah, speaking in harmony with blessed Paul, says: "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." From Isaiah you have one image. Come with me now to another image. See the truth shining through the types. The serpents were biting the children of Israel when the people had fallen into ruin. Moses begs God to give a remedy for their salvation. God shows his servant a remedy of kindness and says: "Make a bronze serpent and set it up before the tent of witness." What does this example mean? Some serpents were biting, and another was crucified on their behalf. What does the riddle mean? What does the shadow of the mystery promise? Just as there in the type, while other serpents were biting, the one that neither bit nor struck was nailed to the wood, so too, while other men sinned, Jesus the sinless was to suffer for all. For the biting serpents a sinless serpent is crucified; for us who are subject to death, he who is not subject to sin is nailed to the cross. Isaiah, among other things, foretold this well, saying something like this: "For the sins of the people he came to death," and: "The Lord handed himself over for our sins." We must state the meaning of the mystery once more. Just as there the biters were some and the one set up on the stake was another, so here all are sinners and one is crucified for all. You have a second image. Consider with me a third image as well, for "on the testimony of two or three witnesses every word shall be established." Why is a bronze serpent crucified? So that the serpents' bites might be made powerless. So the one crucified is one thing, and what is made powerless is another. Do you not see the reflection of the truth? Do you not see the power of the dispensation, as if in hidden writing? The serpent was crucified, it says, so that the biters' bites might be made powerless. Christ was crucified so that the workings of the demons might be made powerless. The serpent set on the stake is one, and the serpents made powerless are others. Christ on the cross is one, and the demons made powerless are others. And just as there the image of the visible serpent made the serpents' bites powerless, so here the death of Christ became the death of death and the overthrow of the demons. Fittingly, then, the Saviour applied the image to himself and said: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." You also have, brother, the blessed Moses sketching the cross in another form. Hear how, for when we speak of the cross we must set out many ways of contemplating the mystery. Once, foreigners attacked the Israelites in the wilderness. The name of these foreigners was Amalek. Moses sends Joshua son of Nun to lead his countrymen in battle. He arms his successor, but he himself stays on the mountain with his hands stretched out. For it says: "Moses went up the mountain and spread out his hands. And whenever Moses stretched out his hands, Israel prevailed; and whenever he lowered his hands" (worn down by the weariness of his body) "Amalek prevailed." What does this posture mean? The Jew, afraid that the glory of Christ's cross might shine out through the image, at once says: "The type has nothing to do with the tales you tell. That posture was a type of prayer, not an image, as you suppose." Then why, if the victory was truly the fruit of prayer, did the text not ascribe the victory to prayer, but to the image and posture of the hands? Scripture did not say, "Whenever Moses prayed," and that truly shows that the victory was not the fruit of prayer. For whenever Moses let his hands down, Israel was defeated; and whenever he spread them out, Amalek was defeated. If this had been the work of prayer, it should have said: "And whenever Moses prayed, he prevailed." But, as I said before, scripture sets prayer aside. It does so not because prayer is useless, but because prayer had to give way to the image of the cross, and it ascribes the victory to the figure and the sign. For "whenever Moses spread out his hands, Israel prevailed." What does an outspread hand mean? Picture to yourself outspread hands, so that you may see the image of the venerable cross shining out. "But Moses grew weary," it says. His hands, overcome by the weight of his body, could no longer keep serving the image. What then? So that the victory would not be undone if the image were undone, Aaron and Hur stand by and hold up his hands. That way the image of the cross would not pass away and cease, and so put out the victory. But why should Aaron and Hur, of all people, support his hands? Aaron, brothers, held priestly rank, and Hur was a kinsman of the royal tribe. So priesthood and kingship serve as a bodyguard to the image of the cross. When the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, Moses and Elijah appeared on his right and on his left to escort the royal image of Christ. In the same way, here too Aaron, who held the rank of the priesthood, escorts the cross, and Hur, who likewise was the first flower of the royal tribe, escorts the cross. I have said these things to show how the image was introduced to those ancient fathers of piety, and how the type of the dispensation was honoured. If those who foretold it proclaimed it so gloriously and prefigured it so honourably, what kind of mouths, and how many and how mighty, will we need to proclaim the Lord's cross and his divine dispensation? I know that a great longing for doctrinal discourses and for preaching on theology has hold of you. But what has been said now is kin to those things. To preach the cross and to exalt the only-begotten God the Word belong to one and the same thought. So whether you sing the praises of the Godhead of the Only-begotten or honour the dispensation, you give one and the same proof of piety.

But when you hear of the cross, when you hear of the dispensation of the body, lift your mind up to the height of the Only-begotten's authority. Do not let the form he took for your sake lower your thoughts. Instead, let the love for humankind of the one who saved you lift your mind up. The cross is for your sake, but the dignity of God belongs to him in his own right. The dignity of God is neither raised up by words nor pulled down by words. Those who pull it down bring about their own downfall, and those who exalt it raise their own lowliness to the heights. As we said before, then, the one who praises the dispensation and the one who praises the theology hold to the same thought. In what we worked through yesterday, however, something was lacking on the text "that they may know you, the only true God, and the Lord Jesus Christ." On "the only true God," the prophecies and testimonies were shown to apply to the Son as well, so that he too is the only true one. But I think it necessary to examine the other part of the phrase as well. And yet the heretic says: "What do you have to say about the one who was sent? It is written expressly: 'and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent.' Does the sender not have a dignity equal in honour to the one sent?" If you read these words as a slave to the letter, you will often find, as we said before, a great deal that truly seems to contradict us. Things that were well written but badly understood will not agree with the same line of reasoning. But if you lift your understanding up to the truth itself, the eye of your mind will nowhere be turned toward contradiction, for it is guided by the Holy Spirit himself to an exact understanding. The words "was sent" and "sent" are human words, but they proclaim divine meanings. The sender did not send from one place to another, nor did the one sent come from one place to another. Yet scripture says, "the Father sent the Son into the world," as though he were not present in the world to which he was being sent. Then how does scripture say of the Lord himself: "He was in the world, and the world came into being through him"? How, then, did the one who was present come? How did the one who was hidden appear? If you really take "he sent" in the sense you hear it, then of necessity the one sent arrived at places where he had not yet been present, and the sender sends him where he himself is not present. How, then, did the evangelist say: "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being. He was in the world, and the world came into being through him"? If, then, he was in the world, how is he sent into the world? Have you not heard him say: "I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord"? What, then, does "was sent" mean? It stands for "was seen," for "shone forth through the flesh." The sending does not mean a passage from place to place, but a passage from invisible Godhead into visible presence. When he sojourned on earth in the human dispensation, he did not empty the heavens of his dignity. Nor now, when he has been taken up in the ascension of the flesh, has he left the earth bereft of his own oversight. If, brothers, the Father sent the Son into the world in the literal sense, then clearly the sender is separated from the one sent in his own location. For if he is with him, "he sent" is superfluous; and if he sent him, he must be separated from him, by the force of the word. But we must not be slaves to the letter; we must keep in step with faith. And what word will testify to us that while he appeared on earth he was in heaven? What word will testify that, though sent by the Father, he was not separated from the Father? If he was sent into the world in the literal sense, if the one who sends is separated from the one sent, how could he say: "I am in the Father and the Father is in me"? And how could he say again: "And the Father who sent me is with me"? You see that the nature is not separated; it is the dispensation that presents the form of a sending. What, then, does "I am going up to my Father" mean? For if the Father is with him, why does he go up? The going up describes the dispensation, the taking up of the body, not a separation in the Godhead. Do you want to learn that, just as when he sojourned on earth he did not leave heaven or become separated from the Father, so when he was taken up to heaven he did not leave the earth bereft? He who said to his disciples, "And see, I am with you," but "I am going up to my Father, from where I came down," also says to them again: "And see, I am with you always, to the end of the age." So the words "that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" have a double meaning, and they are a double-edged sword. One edge is armed against idolatry, and the other is drawn up in battle against the unbelief of the Jews. He says "the only true God" to denounce the dead idols, and "Jesus Christ whom you have sent" to silence those who deny the dispensation. So take the words according to their sense, and do not insult his dignity because of how they are worded.

To learn exactly that being sent by God does not mean moving from place to place but revealing the dispensation, consider what the Gospel says about John the Baptist, who was from the earth: "There was a man sent from God." Was John sent from heaven, then? Did he come from above? How then did he come? A man who is sent does not move from place to place; he is entrusted with a dispensation. And if God the Word, who fills all things, says that he has been sent, has he insulted his own nature, when he was only making the dispensation known? Look at him, brother: he fulfils the dispensation of the flesh, and he does not lower the dignity of his divine power. Consider also his priestly role: "I go up to my Father, and I will entreat him, and he will send you an Advocate, the Spirit of truth." If you go up on high and entreat, and in entreating implore, and after the entreaty send the Spirit (for you said, "I entreat, and I send"), why do you set aside the Father's authority before your ascent? If you do not act on your own authority as divine dignity allows, but wait to go up to the Father in heaven, offer entreaty and supplication, and so receive the grace of the Spirit and send it out into the whole world, why do you show an authority of your own before you ascend and before you entreat? Why, before the ascension, once you had risen from the dead, did you breathe into the faces of the apostles and say, "Receive the Holy Spirit"? What you ask of the Father, you give before you have made your supplication to the Father. Are you only pretending to ask, then? "I am not pretending," he says, "for there is no pretence in the truth. One thing befits the dignity, the other suits the dispensation." Why then did you breathe into the faces of the apostles? "Having risen from the dead," says the Saviour, "I had to give the world the firstfruits of life. When Adam was formed he received the breath of life (for God breathed into Adam's face, and he became a living soul). What he received and lost, I now come and call back. I raise up the fallen, I renew the corrupted, I give life to the one who was put to death. The prophet too bears witness to my dispensation, for he proclaimed my breathing aloud." And which prophet cries out and foretells this holy breathing? "Listen," he says, "to the prophet who speaks among the Twelve, whose name is Nahum: 'Keep your feasts, O Judah; pay your vows to God; they shall no more come again into oldness. It is finished.'" First he says: "They shall no more come again into oldness." Here he announces the good news of the new grace: the old things have ceased, and the new are in bloom. "Keep your feasts." Why does he say "keep the feast"? Because the resurrection was to blossom at the feast of the Passover. "Keep your feasts, O Judah," he says, "pay your vows to God. They shall no more come again into oldness. It is finished, it is taken away." That is, the former things are at an end. And why are the former things at an end? "For he has come up from the earth who breathes into your face and rescues you from affliction." But let us take it up again. "Keep your feasts, O Judah; pay your vows to God. They shall no more come again into oldness." What are these feasts? Those old feasts bore the image of the new ones. First comes the day of Unleavened Bread, which to anyone who looks closely is an image of the passion. After it comes the day of Pentecost, which is likewise an image of the coming of the holy and adorable Spirit. And the feast of Tabernacles, too, was an image of the heavenly tabernacles. The Lord pointed to such things as well. Since those tents were temporary, and he wanted to show that they were a type of the tents to come, he said to those who are rich in this world: "Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when it fails they may welcome you into the eternal tents." The temporary tents, then, were a type of the eternal tents. Since the dispensation of Christ fulfilled the old types and brought the new grace into bloom, the prophet was right to foretell it, saying: "Keep your feasts, O Judah; pay your vows to God." "They shall no more come again into oldness" means that the old things have been renewed through grace. "It is finished, it is taken away. For he has come up from the earth who breathes into your face and rescues you from affliction." The prophet Nahum, then, has plainly set before you the Lord who breathed the holy grace into us. Isaiah too, in a different way, foretells the one who rose from the dead and bestows the Holy Spirit on his own. He says: "He remembered the days of old, he who brought up from the earth the shepherd of the sheep." And in place of "he breathed into his face" he at once adds: "he who put the Holy Spirit within them." The divine dignity, the divine title, the royal rank, the spotless glory and the incomprehensible power: that which is glorified together with the Father, reigns together with the Son, works all things, and distributes the divine gifts to each one as it wills. I know well that these words strengthen the Church's own, but they sting and tear apart her enemies, above all the enemies of true religion, who refuse to glorify the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son. What wretchedness! They will not grant the Holy Spirit even what they themselves have received. Yet the apostle said of himself and those like him: "If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him." Paul is glorified together with God, and the Spirit [?] is not glorified together with him? Mortal nature is raised so high that it is glorified together with Christ, and will the adorable Spirit not share even the privileges we share? The same apostle says of human beings: "If we endure, we shall also reign with him." Does the Holy Spirit not reign with Christ? What gross ingratitude! What great and intolerable madness! What a godless opinion, what boundless blasphemy, what an incurable wound! We expect to reign with him, and we put the Holy Spirit in the rank of a slave?

We say this, brothers, not as if the Holy Spirit were to be glorified with Christ in the same way we are, but to expose the impiety of people who will not grant it even that much. Be merciful to us, Lord, for what we are saying. Even if we repeat the words of the impious, only as bare and superficial wording, let no one think, brothers, that repeating their insults is itself an insult to the Holy Spirit. We bring those insults into the open and speak them, not because we share in the impiety, but to expose the error and to wall off those raised in true religion from wicked doctrines. The apostles, too, loved the Lord and had seen his dignity, yet they did not shrink from putting the insults of the Jews into the holy Gospels. All that the Jews dared to say about Christ is written there: that he is a sinner, and that he is not from God. And they did not shrink from saying to his face: "You are a Samaritan and have a demon." But the fact accuses those who blasphemed, not those who wrote it down. Hear the working of the Spirit; hear the apostles' doxology; walk by their teaching; follow in the steps of the saints; do not lead yourself astray in the tracks of the profane. Worship the Trinity; glorify the Trinity; proclaim the Trinity. This is how the prophets think, how the apostles preach, how the martyrs believe. Hear Paul proclaiming the Trinity: "There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; varieties of workings, but the same God who works all things in all." Why does he not begin with the Father? Why does he not proclaim the Father first, then the Son, and after him the Holy Spirit? Are you changing the order, Paul? Are you rearranging the sequence? The Saviour handed down "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit": are you overturning the rule of theology? God forbid that we should ever think such things of Paul. That holy and wonderful herald saw clearly that even if he mentions the Spirit first, he keeps theology unharmed: he does not insult the unconfused nature, and he does not divide the undivided dignity. He mentions the Spirit first to show that being written last does not make the Spirit last and least. Those people interpret wrongly: they do not count the Son together with the Father, or the Holy Spirit together with the Son, but count each beneath the other. "First," they say, "comes the Father, second the Son, third the Holy Spirit." They do not understand the well-ordered sequence in which we come to know the adorable Trinity; with a perverted soul they lay hands on the purity of theology. So Paul is right to reverse the order of the names, to show the power of the truth and undo what the wicked suppose. "But I know," says the heretic, "that he mentioned the Son and the Spirit only in passing, but when he came to the Father he raised theology to its height. Of the Spirit he said, 'the same Spirit'; of the Son, 'the same Lord'; but when he came to the Father he said, 'who works all things in all.'" What then? Does the phrase "works all things in all" indicate sovereign authority to you? "Yes," he says. And does it proclaim surpassing preeminence? "Yes," he says. I accept your admissions, provided you stand by the terms. Let us see, then, what the chosen vessel, steered by the Holy Spirit, sets out more clearly on this very question. "To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one is given a word of wisdom through the same Spirit; to another a word of knowledge in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing by the same Spirit; to another prophecy; to another interpretation of tongues; to another faith; to another gifts. All these..." Pay close attention. See how both the words and the power agree. Earlier he had said, "the same God who works all things in all"; now, when he comes to the Spirit, he attests this same power to the Spirit: "All these," he says, "are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each individually as it wills." So the harmony of the doxology is not broken when one of the names of the holy Trinity is placed first, second or third. First, second and third do not indicate a difference of nature; they mark an unconfused path of theology. Again, the same apostle wants to show that he uses the order of the names without distinction everywhere, while still approaching the divine proclamation in good order and on firm ground. So, writing to the Thessalonians, he says: "Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father..." Are you proclaiming the Son first, Paul, and then the Father? "You have put the first out of its order," someone says. "If I say first and second, I take the nature to be undivided. Or rather, I do not merely suppose it; I proclaim it with certainty." So do not insult the divine oracles, and do not slander the heavenly doctrines. You find a similar image in the Old Testament too. Here Paul began from the Spirit, came to the Son, and from the Son went on to the Father, making the name that is third in order first. He did not change the order of the proclamation; he showed that in theology the order makes no difference. In the same way you will find this pattern shining in advance in the Old Testament, as if in an image. Which of us does not know, brothers, that Scripture puts Abraham first, Isaac second and Jacob third? "I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." Scripture rightly names the begetter first, then the begotten, then the one born of him. But since their nature was undivided, even though the succession of generations separated them in time, God did not hesitate to change the order, in order to show their accord. In Leviticus he says (I give the passage as well, so that you cannot slander what is said): "If the children of Israel sin, I will hand them over to a foreign nation, and they will go there and serve other gods." Foretelling the captivity in Babylon, he says: "And they will go there and serve other gods. Then their uncircumcised heart will be put to shame." And shortly afterwards: "And they will remember the covenant of Jacob and the covenant of Isaac and the covenant of Abraham."

I will repeat the passage, because the applause drowned out the subject. "There," he says, "their uncircumcised heart will be put to shame, and they will turn back to me, and I will heal them." No sooner the threat than he promises reconciliation. "And I will bring them back to the land of their fathers, and I will remember the covenant of Jacob and the covenant of Isaac and the covenant of Abraham." Do you see how he changes the order to show their equal honour? He did not make Jacob first in time; he used the order freely, to show their equal honour. With the patriarchs, though, time separates the fruit from the root, for both the offspring and their parents are mortal by nature. But the nature of the holy, immortal and adorable Trinity is not cut by any reasoning, not divided by any time, not separated by any ages. There is nothing between the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Only-begotten is the maker of the ages. Hear the divine and noble herald saying something of this kind about the Father: "In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages." There is nothing, then, between the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit: no time, and no interval of time. The Father is before the ages; the Son is before the ages, for he himself made the ages; the Holy Spirit is before the ages. Nowhere is the nature split; nowhere is the power divided. Pay close attention. The Father reigns, the Son reigns, the Holy Spirit reigns. I know I have used this proof before, but saying the same things is no burden to me, and it is a safeguard for you. The Father reigns, as it says: "Our God is King for ever." The Son reigns: "The Lord will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever." The Holy Spirit reigns. Isaiah said: "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of hosts, sitting on a throne high and lifted up. And he said to me: Go and say to this people: You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive," and so on. The apostle takes the prophet's theology as referring to the Holy Spirit. The prophet had said, "I saw the King, the Lord of hosts, and he said to me: Go and say to this people." Paul takes "King, Lord of hosts" to mean the Holy Spirit, and when he is debating with the Jews in Rome he says: "The Holy Spirit spoke well to our fathers through the prophet Isaiah, saying: Go and say to this people: You will indeed hear but never understand," and so on. Isaiah said, "I saw the King of hosts, and he said to me: Say to this people." And Paul, by saying this, ascribed the authority to the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, then, is King and Lord of hosts, the one who said to Isaiah: "Go and say to this people: You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive," and so on. For "I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go and say to this people." The Father is Lord; the Son is Lord: "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand." The Holy Spirit is Lord: "The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Let no one think that the name "God" is greater because it comes first, and the name "Lord" lesser because it comes second. Of the immortal nature both "Lord" and "God" are said, and even if the two words do not have the same meaning, they proclaim the same dignity. Well then: is "God" the first name? If "Lord" were second, Moses would not have used the second as if it were first, saying: "The Lord your God, the Lord is one." If that were so, he ought to have mentioned the first name first and said, "Your God, the Lord, is one." But to show that it makes no difference which name comes first, he said "Lord" first and then "God." But let us return to our subject. "Now the Lord is the Spirit." The Father, then, is Lord, the Son is Lord, the Holy Spirit is Lord. "But Paul says, 'one Lord.'" If there is one Lord, how is there Lord and Lord? Clearly, the lordship is one. In the same way there is one God, as Paul says: "For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." "So then," says the heretic, "he called the Father God and the Son Lord." Let us see, brothers, let us see, I beg you, whether "Lord" is a secondary name of the divine dignity, or whether it is truly both first and fitting, and attested by holy Scripture. It really is necessary for us to speak with care, for you to listen with eagerness, and for them to be taught the truth. What passage, then, will testify for us that the name "Lord" is both first and proper to the majestic glory? Hear the prophet David: "Let them be put to shame and troubled for ever and ever; let them be confounded and perish. And let them know that your name is Lord." The enemy may say that this was said of the Saviour, the Word: Christ's name is Lord, the Father's name is God. Once again I demand that we fix the terms of the question. Do you hold to the heretics' argument? Do you stand by the terms? I fear your shiftiness. When you are refuted, you flee from this truth to another interpretation; and when you are caught there too, you flee to yet another piece of folly, when you ought not to flee the truth that shines and gives light. The truth that gives light does not drive anyone away; rather, "the wicked flee when no one pursues."

But let us return to our subject. "Let them know that your name is Lord." If he is speaking of the Father, then learn that the Father's name is Lord. And if the Father's name is Lord, Paul says: "One Lord, Jesus Christ." So the Father is Lord, and the Son is Lord. Since the Son shares the name, he shares the dignity too. But the Jew declines this, and says that it was not said of the Father, so that by assigning "Lord" to the Son he may keep "God" for the Father. I accept the terms and the condition. As I have often said before, I do not divide the dignity of the names of the adorable Trinity, because the Church holds its glory undivided. But I will stoop to your wretched level and say: let it be granted that "Let them know that your name is Lord" refers to the Son. What then will you do with the words that follow: "You alone are Most High over all the earth"? By your feeble reasoning and your teaching, the Father is no longer the Most High, because the Son alone is Most High. Here, brothers, these are not waves of the sea that drown, but waves of love that sanctify. Yet while Christ is being spoken of and proclaimed, let this God-loving vessel keep calm. It would be absurd if the sea, which saw the Master's footsteps and heard "Peace, be still," respected his authority, while the Church did not heed her own Bridegroom as he speaks the words of life and truly has divine grace on his lips: "Grace is poured out on your lips." But let us return to our subject. "Let them know that your name is Lord." Choose whichever you like, though not as if the choice were in your power. When Joshua son of Nun said to the people, "Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, the gods your fathers served or the Lord our God," he did not put the choice entirely in human power; he wanted to show that true religion follows the free choice of those who love God. And elsewhere the same man says: "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord, to serve him." There the choice did not insult God's dignity; it showed the free choice of the devout. In the same way, if I now leave the choice to your free will, I am not insulting the dignity but testing the choice. Was "Let them know that your name is Lord" said of the Father or of the Son? If it was said of the Father, and the Father's name is Lord, then the Son's name is also Lord, for there is "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." So the rank is common to both, like the name. But if "Lord" is the Son's name, then the Son alone is Lord, for "you alone are Most High over all the earth." In that case, since the Son is the one and only Lord, is the Father a stranger to lordship? God forbid! When the Father is proclaimed the one and only God, the Son is not cast out of the Godhead either: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Calling the Father God, then, does not shut the Son out of the Godhead, for "the Word was God." Nor, when the Son is called "one Lord," does this show the Father to be a stranger to lordship, for "the Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand." So the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, the Holy Spirit is Lord, for "the Lord is the Spirit." But the heretic raises his head again in irritation, and when he hears the Holy Spirit called Lord he bursts with rage. "How," he says, "is the Spirit [?] Lord, when, speaking through the prophet David, it sings the praise of the Son with the words, 'The Lord said to my Lord'? Do you see," he says, "that the Spirit speaking through the prophet confesses both the Father and the Son as its Lord?" What then, brothers? Now that this phrase has been raised, it must not become more ambiguous for the listeners. So I will turn to the examination of the passage itself and set out for you the whole meaning of the phrase.

Once, when the Savior was in conversation with the synagogue of the Jews and testing what opinion and belief most people held about him, he said to them: "Whom do you say the Christ is? Whose son is he?" The scribes and the Pharisees said: "David's." Then the Lord, setting himself against their assumption, went on: "How then does David, in the Holy Spirit, call him Lord? For 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.'" He added "in the Holy Spirit" not to prove the Spirit a servant of the Christ who was being proclaimed. He added it to show clearly that the prophet, foreseeing the future in the Holy Spirit, truly confesses as Lord the one who was to be his son according to the flesh. The question put to the Lord was not about the Holy Spirit but about himself: does David have the Lord as his son or as his master? Indeed, the Lord himself forestalled the slander of the heretics and kept the dignity of the Holy Spirit intact, settling the dispute with what he added next. What does he say? "If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" He did not say, "If then the Holy Spirit calls him Lord," but, "If David calls him Lord." Why then did he add "in the Holy Spirit calls him Lord"? Because to speak of Christ before Christ's coming was not the work of a body that sees, but of the Holy Spirit showing things in advance. David did not proclaim what he saw. What the Holy Spirit suggested to him, he struck out on the spiritual lyre. That is why the Lord added: "How then does David, in the Holy Spirit, call him Lord?" But so that the heretic might not drag his blasphemy over to the Holy Spirit, he went on again, as we have already said: "If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" So it is David who, in the Holy Spirit, calls Christ Lord. But let us first consider this: every prophet, as is fitting, speaks from the Holy Spirit. For we all confess that the prophets spoke in the Holy Spirit, as the apostle also testifies: "The Holy Spirit spoke rightly to your fathers through the prophet." And again God says, speaking of all: "I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh, and they shall prophesy." And Moses: "Would that all the people were prophets, that the Lord would put his Holy Spirit upon them!" Here let us pay close attention to how the divinity of the Holy Spirit is shown. It is not exalted by us; it is proclaimed by its own dignity. Allow me for a little while to set out the matter as question and answer, for by such exchanges of objection and reply the solution to difficulties becomes easier. Let us ask, then: do they confess that the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophets, or do they still disbelieve and doubt? If they doubt, let us remind them of what was said above, how God himself testifies: "I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh, and they shall prophesy." For it is the Spirit who brings about the power of prophecy. So too the wonderful Moses, wishing to show that prophecy comes from the Holy Spirit, broke out with that great and wonderful cry: "Would that all the Lord's people were prophets, that the Lord would put his Holy Spirit upon them!" But if they truly confess, as is indeed true, that the Holy Spirit spoke in the prophets, then hear how the blessed and wonderful Zechariah, father of the Forerunner, calls the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets God: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited his people and brought them redemption, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets of old." So it was God who spoke through the mouth of the prophets, and it was the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophets, as David says in the Second Book of Samuel: "For the Spirit of the Lord spoke in me." Then the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets is God and Lord. Take a clear proof of what I am saying. The divine apostle, wishing to show that the Holy Spirit is in the prophetic voice, says in the letter to the Corinthians: "If all prophesy, and an outsider or unbeliever comes in, he is convicted by all and examined by all, and the secrets of his heart are laid bare. And so, falling on his face, he will worship, declaring that God is truly among you." Do you see that the teacher of true religion expressly proclaimed the Spirit in those who prophesy to be God?

Why then do you stumble over true religion, heretic? Why do you slander the dignity of the Spirit? Why do you break the confession of faith? Read again the covenant you made at the mysteries, and how you said: "I believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit." Have you torn down what you believed? Have you overturned what you confessed? Have you now impiously muddied what you once made plain and pure? Do you make war on peace? Do you fight against your own covenant? Have you denied the faith, and do you now bring in disputes? The gift was handed to you as one who believed and confessed, and after the gift is faith banished and debate brought in? Do not insult the dignity of grace. Do not counterfeit the covenant of that fearful and awe-inspiring initiation. You confessed that you believe in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. In the same way you were baptized into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The blessing likewise is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Do we receive gifts from grace, while from you grace receives blasphemy? From the Holy Spirit do we receive freedom, while from you the Spirit receives slavery? What madness! What ingratitude! Either renounce the new grace, or respect the old covenant, or everywhere set forth the equal honor of the holy Trinity, as we have often shown you through many written testimonies. To these I wish to add yet another proof. For, as I have often said, the new things were announced beforehand in the old. What then does God command Moses? He says: "Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus shall you bless the children of Israel." Pay close attention. He laid down the word "thus" so that no one would casually assume that any form of blessing was fine. No one was to deliver blessings by his own authority, but everything was to be done according to the rule of Scripture. "Thus," he says, "bless." Thus—how? "The Lord bless you and keep you." Note how everywhere he introduces the Trinity in a hidden way, and through the Trinity the blessings are made threefold: "The Lord bless you and keep you. The Lord make his face shine upon you and bless you. The Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace." See the Trinity expressly hymned. What grace does not come from the Holy Spirit? What gift does not come from him? What good thing is there without him? What could appear to human beings from beyond this world without the Holy Spirit? Search the Scriptures and consider how, whenever Scripture wants to indicate or show something done beyond nature, it ascribes the whole of it to the authority of the Spirit. Take Samson, that noble champion. When he performed those great and astonishing feats of courage, Scripture showed it everywhere by placing the Holy Spirit before his exploits. Foreigners came against Samson, it says, many beyond counting. He was alone, and not only alone but bound. What release was there for the bound man? What rescue for the one who was trapped? How could one man prevail over many? "The Spirit of the Lord came down upon Samson, and he leapt upon the foreigners, and finding the jawbone of a donkey, he killed a thousand men." See the wisdom of divine Scripture. Those who did not know the man would find the story unbelievable, that the bound man defeated men who were free and the one prevailed over the many. So Scripture rightly put first: "And the Spirit of the Lord came upon Samson, and he took a donkey's jawbone and killed a thousand." What is beyond belief because of human nature would then be believed because of the power of the Spirit. So Moses rightly said: "How could one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless the Lord had handed them over and God had sold them?" Read the Scriptures and you will find the authority of the Spirit placed before every exploit. The foreigners came, and the Spirit of the Lord came down upon Samson. A lion sprang at him, and he tore the lion apart as one would a young goat. He was bound with iron chains, and the woman said to him: "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But again Scripture says: "And the Spirit of the Lord came upon Samson, and the bonds came apart like tow when it catches the scent of fire." Nowhere did Scripture introduce a single feat of valor without first setting down the working of the Spirit. Then, when at last he was stripped of his power, pay close attention to what divine Scripture has handed down. Everywhere, when he was leading and conquering, it says: "The Spirit of the Lord came upon Samson." When his head was shaved and he gave away the pledge of grace, it at once wrote: "And the Lord departed from Samson." When the foreigners came: "And the Spirit of the Lord came down upon him." When the Spirit withdrew, it says: "And the Lord departed from him." And rightly so, for the Lord is the Spirit. You will find this insight not only in the Old Testament but also in the Acts of the Apostles. Whenever the divine oracles proclaim some great and surpassing power, they everywhere put the authority of the Spirit first. Scripture presents Paul in Cyprus punishing with a word that accursed Elymas the magician, who was waging war against the truth. Since it was about to relate something strange, eyes put out by a word, it says: "For behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind, unable to see the sun." This went beyond the nature of Paul and of every human being—I mean, to destroy someone's eyes by a human word. A human word does not change nature or blind the sight. So that no one would look only at the human words, be bewildered by what happened, and think the account mistaken, Scripture again puts the authority of the Spirit first: "Then Paul," it says, "filled with the Holy Spirit, said to him." You have another proof of the Spirit as well: when an unlearned man speaks beyond his ability. Here too Scripture ascribes the working to the Spirit. For example, Peter and John address the crowd of the Jews, and "then," it says, "Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to the people: Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge." Why then "filled with the Holy Spirit"? Because such boldness was beyond an unlearned man. Someone looking at the fisherman might disbelieve the boldness of the holy word, so Scripture put the wisdom of the Holy Spirit first, so that you would not be astonished at what was supplied. Let us consider one more example, if you please, so that what has been said may be confirmed all the more clearly. Heaven is opened to the saints, but without the Holy Spirit it is not opened. Heaven opening is not seen with eyes of flesh but through the working of the Holy Spirit. Stephen saw the heavens opened, but, as Scripture says, he saw them because he was full of the Holy Spirit. Nowhere, then, brothers, can anyone see heaven opened without the Spirit. Nor can anyone take on the authority to teach, or display the power of miracles, without the holy and adorable Spirit. For one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually as he wills. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
